chunks: Designing a board for reworkability. The question: What can you do in your design to improve reworkability?
Designing for reworkability means laying out a board so that someone can later remove and replace a part without ruining the board.
In practice that means leaving room for the repair tool, letting heat reach the joint you want to melt, and building in options so a fix is a part swap instead of a wire.
Think of a house built to be repaired. There is open space around the water heater, an access panel in the wall, and labeled shutoff valves.
Boxed in behind drywall, the same heater still works, but fixing it means tearing things apart. A board is the same.
The dashed square is the area a rework nozzle (plus its airflow margin) occupies.
On the left, a tall capacitor and small passives sit inside it, so they would be heated, blown or shadowed. On the right the zone is clear and the same parts sit outside it.
Ask your assembler for nozzle sizes; the margin is typically a few millimetres around the part but is equipment dependent.
Keepout: an empty area left around a part so a tool can reach it. Nozzle: the tip of a hot-air tool that blows hot air onto a part to melt its solder.
Thermal relief: a pad joined to a big copper area through thin spokes, so less heat drains away.
DNP (do not populate): a footprint (the set of pads a part sits on) left empty on purpose so a part can be fitted later.
Zero-ohm link: a resistor of 0 ohms used as a jumper you can remove. BGA: a chip whose connections are small solder balls hidden underneath it.
Take a 15 mm BGA. Say the repair nozzle needs 3 mm of clear space on every side. The clear zone is then 15 + 3 + 3 = 21 mm across.
A tall capacitor 2 mm from the BGA sits inside that zone and would be heated or blocked, so you move it outside.
You also add an empty footprint for a second resistor, so changing a value later is a part swap, not a wire.
Heavy parts on the back side are another risk: melted solder may not hold them. That is the whole idea.

"I'd leave keepouts around BGAs and big parts so a nozzle can sit there, keep tall parts away, add thermal reliefs on plane-connected signal pins, and put alternate footprints and zero-ohm links where I expect changes.
I'd keep heavy parts off the bottom under rework areas because they can fall during reheat, avoid hiding parts under BGAs, add test points to diagnose faults, and mark pin 1 and polarity clearly."
Quick check. Why leave a keepout around a BGA?
